THE WAR-TRAIL. a romance. »Y CAl'TAIN RIAYNE R HID. chapter lxxix. a subterranean fire. In the midst of my meditations, night descended upon the earth. It promised to be a moonless uigbt. A robe of sable clouds formed a sombre lining to the sky, and through this neither moon nor stars were visible. It grew darker apace, until in the dim light I could scarcely distinguish the forms of my companions þÿ neither men nor horses, though both were near me. The men were still asleep, stretched along the grass in various attitudes, like so many bodies upon a battlefield. The horses were too hungry to sleep þÿ ' the constant crop-crop' told that they were greedily browsing upon the sward of gramma-grass that, by goodfortune, grew luxuriantly around. This would be the best rest for them, and I was glad to thiuk that this splendid provender would in a few hours recruit their strength. It was the chonilrosium fatneum, the favourite food of horses and cattle, and in its effects upon their condition almost equal to the bean or the oat. I knew it would soon freshen the jaded animals, and make them ready for the road. At least in this there was some consolation. We are happy to see, that, at length, some tribute has been paid to the Rector for his indefatigable exertions in the erection of that beautiful edifice, St. John's Church ; which is undeniably the greatest ornament of our Island. Not only the thanks of his congregation, but those of the whole community, are due to him for having accomplished so much with such small means; and we may venture to offer the assurance, that this community will ever remain grateful for that zeal which he has always evinced in a good cause.
St. Croix. July 10th 1858.

Warmly attached to the people among whom I have labor, d for the last 12 years, and giveh the flower of my life to promote all objects for the improvement of the moral, social and religious condition of the community, it affords me great satisfaction to be assured by my official co-laborers that my course meets with their unanimous approval and warm appreciation. years of unremitting toil a Vestry of faithful and ; longer deferred. trust-worthy laymen, who by unity of action and thus aided in the accomplishment of the wise counsels, have smoothed our pat' . and I rejoice that they are still witli us to than,. God and to bliss God for all that has been done and to pray for a further outpouring ot bis Grace. And 1 regard it as an especial reason for thankfulness to God, that I have been spared and strengthened to pass through, unaided and alone, the heavy duty that has pressed upon me in this large parish and at tlie last to see the completion of its Church and Schools With many thanks for all your kindness and sympathy towards one so unworthy, 1 would especialU i: voke the blessing of Almighty God upon each one of you and your families, and upon all who by their offerings or their prayers, have aided us in accomplishing a work which must exercise on ourselves and succeeding generations an influence for lasting good, the value of which it is impossible for us to overrate. ( From the London Times , July 14.) There is a character so common in popular stories that it must address itself to a very general ambition. It is the young fellow whose quick sympathies are happily assisted with health, strength, and a slight acquaintance with the noble art of defence, and who seldom appears on the scene without finding a victim to be rescued and a ruffian to be knocked down. The ruffian is always a rough, burly brute, inaccessible to reason, yielding to no argument but force, and judging of men by their exterior The champion is slight, hut active, wiry, and invincible in his rage If for one instant lie appeals to the reason or the better feelings of the wrongdoer, it is only that the, novelist may thereby aggravate the crime and further justify the avenger. The result is delightful, and dull indeed is the reader who does not wish fur similar powers and opportunities of doing good Hut when the transport of admiration is over it may still occur that that is not the ordinary way in which good is done in this world. A pugilistic encounter in the streets must he re garded as an exceptional occurrence. Fisti cuffs arc not the daily bread of moral life. The greater part of mankind, be their spirit ever so high, are not a match for a drunken paviour, or for the meanest adept of the prize ring. The good that is done is by other means. It is hy tact, gentleness, p rsuasion, by the evidence of sincerity, and the inducements of kindness, that most people must do the littb good they can ever hope to do This is the

gentle force, this the art of defence open to all, and not dependent on youth or sex, on sinew or hone. It has not to go into tlie streets for its opportunities, and does not require for the good of one being the destruction or injury of another. On the contrary, it does good all round. Having admitted that the more popular ideal of benevolence deals with blows rather than words, and must have a victim, as well as an object, we are painfully aware that we stand at adisad vantage in disputing Lord Palmerston's view- of national duty in regard to the Slave Trade His speech ir so thoroughly imbued with the popular idea that we are inclined to think he has been relieving his unofficial ennui with a series of light reading from the circula tiug libraries He sallies forth into the streets determined to find somebody whom it is neces

sary to knock down. There is only' one way of dealing with mankind. þÿDon talk t of the improved sentiment of Brazil, though it has given up the Slave Trade. It only yielded to force. þÿDou talk t of Spain ever listening to argument. She listens to none but that of guus, and reads truth only' in our flag. Taught by force, indeed, and ruled with a rod of iron, even Spain, after the example of Brazil, may eventually acquire a spontaneous humanity ; j but it must go through a hard tutelage, and England must be her master. As for France, þÿ well, how about France ? Lord Palmerston dexterously reserves France for the peroration «.f his speech, to illustrate the influence of our example. Having demonstrated by Spain and Brazil that we could do nothing but by force, he finally brings in France to augment the splendour of the icsult, but omits to explain whether we won France to our cause þÿby what he had previously laid down to be the only means of doing good. Then ns for the United States, there again we arc left in the dark. It is evident that fhe United States remain to be converted, but whether by broadsides or by gentler means Lord Palmerston dues not say'. The argument rests, then, on the solitary example of Brazil, and it involves the supposition that, but for our squadrons, and the Act of Parliament which sets those squadrons in motion, every port of Brazil would become a mart of the Slave Trade. The hate statement of facts, then, is far from encouraging. One State alone has been converted by Lord Pal-

þÿmerston only s argument, and that one conversion is hollow, unwilling, and only waiting for the withdrawal of the sharp eye and cutting lash. Meanwhile, there are nations to whom the argument of force is inapplicable, and Lord Palmerston has no mode of appealing to them. On his own showing, therefore, this one argument is bankrupt. As Brazil then, is but an inadequate basis to support the theory of conversion þÿby force, Lord Palmerston brings in Africa herself. His argument here stands thus The African chiefs must have money and European commodities. If we let them alone, they will get these by every now and then surrounding a Village, and marching tin inhabitants several hundred miles i to the nearest , slave-port. If we stop i L is traffic they will take to other means of raising a 1 icvenne, and bring cotton, palm-oil, and ivory t" th Coast instead of men, wonion, and children Now, this is a very old question ; it is < ne which p esents itself in many foims; but experience has always answered it far otherwise than Lord Palmerston does in this instance. \\ e þÿdon m t ake good men by punishing bad men. We þÿdon create t good trades by stopping bad ones. Hallows, gaols, hulks, and public works may be necessary, but other institutions, other persuasives, are necessary for sociil improvement of a positive character. If v t want to civilize Africa we must begin at the right end, by taking all the steps in the power of Government and compatible with sound principles to develope a peaceful trade with

tie interior of Africa. No doubt that will tend to supersede the traffic in slaves, and maydo so very quickly ; where is, the most vigilant watching by British cruisers on the coast can only have a negative influence. It can onlydo a remote good to struggle with an immediate wrong i All this time, if we really wish to stop the Slave 1 rade, and arc ready to sacrifice our national jealousies to that, object, we have hinted at a most effectual course The already United States are, unfortunately, not above allowing the irregular use of their flag in the Slave Trade between Africa and Cuba. But thev stand rather too high in the scale of nations as well as in their own esteem to permit a Slave Trade into their own ports. Luba once an ncxed, the whole trade comes to an end, and not a port will remain open where the slaver < ati land his wretched cargo. Spain has long since forfeited all absolute claim to our inter position in her behalf. Indeed, by this time, we presume she would rather not he assisted by ns, be the cause good or bad. Are we, then, prepared to make this sacrifice of national leeling for the sake of that philanthropy which we are always preaching to the world at the point of the bay onet and the mouth of cannon ? \V e ask no reply- ; we only suggest that if England chooses to regard the Slave Trade as the greatest of human crimes, and its extinction an object worth fleets, quarrels, and wars,

We only wish that Spain could e w-a ned in time ; but warning is not for Spain H d she listened to warning, she might still have stood in the first class of nations. But, as far as Spain is concerned, we must bow to Lord Palmerston's authority. She only regards force. Unfortunately, with all our cruisers, we have not tiro same leverage upon her as that in the hands of our American cousins. We may vainly attempt to watch her ports and scrutinize her traffic; once they step in, they will wipe out not only the Slave Trade, but Cuba itself, from the list of Spanish iniquities.

It is founded on the well-known property of lime which combines with fatty substances, whether free or transformed into alkaline soaps. When the saccharute of lime is brought into contact with a dissolution of soap or soda, the sugpr is set at libet ty, the lime combines with the acid of soap, and the soda remains in dissolution in the liquid. When the clarification has been

effected with an excess of lime, and the liquid has been skimmed a first time, it must be allowed to cool below 104 deg. Fahrenheite ; the solution of soap is then poured into the liquid, being gently stirred all the while. When the whole has been well incorporated, it is brought again to the boiling point, after which the temperature is suddenly lowered again, by the suppression of the steam current, aud the new scum is removed. The latter consists entirely of a calcareous soap, which iu rising to the surface has carried away with it till rite impurities and extraneous substanci's co aim I in tin liquid, and has an excellent taste. This process requires no new apparatus, increases the beauty of the augur, yields more, and is consequently more economical.

Somk years ago, tbe subject of emigration of free labourers to this Island occupied the serious attention of our Planters and others interested in the welfare of the Island. The Colonial Council advised the passing of a law empowering the Burgher Council to raise loans to defray the expenses connected with an emigration of a sufficient number of labourers to supply the demand

ft IN. ft B ft d « |y ft d ft. felt to be increasing year by year. The law received His Majesty's sanction on the 13th September 1855 ; but lias not as yet been put into operation. During the debates on the subject, in the Burgher and Colonial Councils, it was, we believe, decided to confine the Emigration to Coolies ; although it was conceded that free African Labourers would be preferable. It was however supposed, that England would interfere to prevent such an emigration, which was then in contemplation by the French Government. Subsequent events have however demonstrated, that England is not quite so Quixotic as to attempt to force the adoption of its moral principles and ideas on other nations. We see then no diliiculty in the way of African Emigration, provided comfortable emigrant ships be obtained and good liiith lie held towards the Emigrants. It will be seen, from another part of our columns, that a greater difficulty has now arisen on the part of the Africans themselves. The cruel manner in which the Emigrants on board tbe French ship Regina Coeli had been treated, led to their rising against the Captain and killing 11 of bis crew. After their capture by tbe English Steamer Etliiope, which took them into Monrovia, they, it is said, made their escape immediately on arriving. The account which they will take with tlieni of their ill-treatment will, no doubt, deter others from any engagement which might be offered them. The practicability of free African Emi gration must now receive a speedy solu-

tion ; and we may well afford to await the ultimate decision which may be arrived at by the French Government. One thing, however, we trust, that our Government, whenever it sanctions such an emigration, will not countenance the reintroduction of any of the many horrors of the slave-trade under the false guise of f ree emigration.

We have the happiness to possess a Government which, if we arc to believe all it tells us, has found means to conciliate Franco without condescending to any of the ordinary means of conciliation, and it is so much our interest to believe it that we are not disposed to weigli probabilities minutely, or call into question what some might consider very doubtful assertions. Let us, then, by all means, take it for granted that our diplomatic feud is at an end, and that a state of feeling has succeeded very different from that which dictated the curt and acrid despatch with which Count Walcwski

concluded the correspondence. I.et us turn our minus to the exploits now ei ctlnp the 1 tropical plains df India, to the orator : an- ' tler launched against us froiu the t- ipk the Capitoline Jove at Washington, to the esti nies of Commissioner Yeh, to tbe blood-stained valleys of Montenegro, or to whatever other quarter may challenge the attention of tin: political observer. Still there is one ofurtnnate fact which will force itself upon our attention in spite of the very beet exertions we can make to persuade ourselves that the political atmospheie is quite as clear on the side of France as we could desire. For what purpose, or in what quarrel, against whom or for whom, we know not, France is undoubtedly arming on a scale, with a method, a system, and deliberation, truly formidable a all her neighbours, þÿ whether, like ourselves, they have the good fortune to be sir tered from the impending storm under the orageous branches of an entente cordiale, þÿ whether, like Belgium, Piedmont, and Spain, in the consei sness of coming tempest,- or whether, like Austria, th know not how soon they may be compelled o reasonable trepidation for 'he first howl of tbe their inability to resist, tl. y listen wit no un- _ fight for their dominions against, a brave and well-disciplined enemy. France i certainly arming, and arming both by land and sea. Her army, already large, is undergoing considerable increase. She is just on the point of completing a railway which connects all her

military stations with the fortifications of Cherbourg, a port constructed at enormous pains and at vast expense, and possessi þÿ eveiy facility that skill can devise for the simultaneous embarcation of very large bodies of troops. France is, besides, busily engaged in the construction of a great steam fleet, armed and prop lied on the very best and in west principles at present developed by tbe art of war; she is gathering up her colossal strength, and would appear to be on the eve of some vast enterprise, in the prosecution of which that strength is to be put forth to the utmost. Not only is tbe military element studiously strengthened and increased, but it is beginning to assert a predominance over civilians which shows itself more and more every day, and naturally makes us anxious about our relations with a country in which the balance is so completely pressed down by the superior weight of the military class. It is in vain that we seek for anything in the present condition of Franco which can account for the remarkable proceedings to which we most unwillingly allude. The finances of the country are in a state that must render tiny naval or militaty expenditure not absolutely called for by necessity or honour peculiarly inexpedient The people of England Imve no wish nearer their hearts than to remain on the very best terms with their formidable and watlike neighbour, and we are sure that there is no country in Europe which would regard a rupture with France with any other feelings

than those of the most genuine abhorrence and dismay. YY'e cannot believe for a moment that the enormous preparations which France is making are intended for defensive warfare, for there is not the slightest symptom of a wish in any quarter to attack Iter. Her form of government agrees entirely with the notions entertained by the Government of tbe greater part of Europe, and we in England have long learnt to renounce the Quixotic notion of forcing our own ideas upon other nations. If France is happy we are content she should be so in her own way, and desire nothing but to see her great, peaceful, and p.osperous Why, then, is France arming ? It may be that the peculiar form of government in which France has seen fit to indulge necessitates some increase of the army for purposes of domestic repression, and we would much rather believe it is so than suppose she is marshalling her forces for some foreign war for ; but, if we grant that the army is increased the purpose of insuring domestic tranquillity, on what ground are we to account for the corresponding and contemporaneous augmentation oflicrileet? The navy has always been a favourite force, in England, because among other reasons, it is a force which cannot readily be used for the purpose of coercing tbe people. In France the same principle must apply, and we are at a loss to know for what pacific pur pose a largo steam navy is being prepared France has but lew colonies, and those of in

considerable extent. She has no large foreign commerce to protect, no refractory India to reconquer and reorganize. She lias nothing to fear from a descent on her coasts from any foreign Power. Why, then, is France arming and augmenting her navy ? We have a right to ask the question; for, whatever be the enemy against whom the thunderbolt is forged, there is 110 doubt that these warlike preparations in a time of profound peace tend to inflict upon us, in common with tho rest d' our neighbours, many of the calamities an 1 miseries ot war. If France will insist on increasing her armies and her navies, she forces us, her neighbours and her allies, to do tho sumo We have too much at stake within this little island of ours to be content to exist by the permission and on the sufferance of any ally, however faithful, þÿ of any foreign Prince, however magnanimous. History warms us ag.iinst incurring the fate of those nations who have trusted the power of the sword in other hands than those in which they were content to trust their freedom. If France is det rmined to arm we must either be content to lie at her mercy or prepare to arm too If ie increases Iter regular army we can hardly d less than call out and embody our Militia. Lt sh isists upon increasing her navy, she "s is m ist unwillingly, from the barest c.o. ide; ations ot prudence, to undergo the expense of a aniiel Fleet. This expenditure, which is not required for domestic purposes, nor for t : defence of our c Ionics, nor

for the reduction of the Indian Rebellion, is purely of the nature of a war expenditure in self-defence, forced upon us by the threatening attitude of a Power which tells us in the same breath that it is our cordial friend mid suie ally. We should prefer other proofs of cordiality, fiiondship, and alliance than are to lie Pound in an attitude which compels us either to trust ourselves blindly and entirely to the professions of a powerful neighbouring State, or to hamper our commerce, embarrass our finances, and retard necessary improvements for t lie purpose of keeping up a barren and unprofitable force to defend us against attacks which may certainly never have been contemplated, but which it is our bouudcii duty t <> render impossible. 1 be time has ar ived wlnwi we ought to speak plainly i a this matt. r. We have had somewhat too much of compliment and grim ace ot late, and a little openness and sincerity on the part ol England would lie refreshing, were it only for their novelty. We would, then, take the liberty respectfully to submit to the Etnpoi or N apoleon that it is tho sincere wish ot this country to lie. his good friend and true ally; that t> this end we have made many sacrifices, and are prepared to make liianv that lie ts at once to enjoy whatever expects more : but he asks too much of us if he power, support, or influence his alliance with England may give linn, and at the same time to inflict upon us by his vast military and naval preparations a War expenditure which wc are most

unwilling to incur, and which casts upon us many of the evils of a state of actual hostilities. In politics many things apparently discordant may be made compatible, but it is impossible that two powerful and neighbouring nations can at the same, time lie arming against each other and united in close alliance and cordial friendship

CHRISTIANSTF.D, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 13 th JULY, 1858. Wf. are indebted to the St. Thomas Times for the interesting letter on the deplorable state of that unfortunate republic, St. Domingo. In reference to the capture of the three Danish vessels, our Government, we learn, have made some representations on the subject ; but with what result, we are unable to state.

Sto. Domingo. St. Dominuo, May, 18j8. My dear Sir, þÿ To give you an idea of the present state of this country I have sketched the following lines: þÿ The blockade announced on the 7th ult. was established at Puerto-Plata on the 23rd; at lloinana no blockade whatever has been established, and at Ar.ua a merely nominal one, for it can hardly be called a blockade where a very tiny schooner and two large boats are placed to prevent the entry of ships, which would be more likely to capture than be captured, þÿ it is a complete farce, for an American schooner ran in there very leisurely and the. blockading squadron pursued her but took good care not to crowd canvas until it was too late. The fleet oft' Puerto Plata is composed of an armed barque under the worthy name of 1 hsn- Incion and six schooners, one of which is called Terror, and most certainly this flotilla of inos. ipiitoes has carried with it terror and dcsoLtion upon every helpless victim that fate drew within the reach of their ravenous clutches. The simple sight of these vessels and their motley crew is sufficient to inspire terror, and I am quite certain, that the first impression þÿ the last also 1 have no doubt þÿ of those who had the misfortune to he captured by them was, that they were a gang of Pirates, and it is only a pity, that some man-of-war from some distant part has not passed that way, for it one had, I am quite positive she would have seized all tb vessels and hung all the crew at the yard arm as Pirates. And they are not better,

for, setting aside their dress, which has not the shadow of the appearance of uniformity or of a navv. the persons who occupy the highest places are notoriously of this class. I will say nothing of the Admiral, for in this line he only begins bis career, (and well be learns bis les Mins,) but bis second in command is one who spent all his early days in high sea piracy, while another officer is a notorious Pirate and highway robber. All the minor officials arc also excellent adepts, and have shown an extraordinary facility for learning their honorable calling. A bombastic intimation to the town of Puerto- Plata to surrender was their first step and it was followed, not by any attack which was too dangerous, hut by flic more easy and more profitable capture of every merchant vessel that attempted to go to that port or even dared to pass in sight of this valiant squadron, commanded by no less a personage than the Minister of War and Marine, who, in his impotent rage at not having succeeded in taking Puerto-Plata by- his terrific intimation, contented himself with treating every ship, every captain, every passenger, and even every sailor in a manner that Pirates would have, been ashamed of: þÿ Mr. Hothe, the Oonsul of Bremen, who was passenger in one, of t he socalled prizes, not having escaped similar treatment, including a voyage of absolute starvation to this port. But would it be consistent with the character of such an exalted man, assisted by such worthy companions, to be satisfied with the
simple savage ill-treatment of defenceless men? Oh no, he, must also plunder every ship of

those things that his capricious cupidity mostly envied. The moment a ship was seized the hatches were broken open, the cargo overhauled þÿ champagne, wine, beer and all other niceties were taken away for the use of the squadron, and as stole their purses, they it was also necessary to till cases of goods of every description which have been sent here for sale, ft was curious to see the Admiral himself with some of his select friends, his Hag captain, sonally superintend these operations, secretary and aide-de-camp, no doubt, with and pertheir own hands breaking open the desks and trunks of the unfortunate passengers in their eager search after gold and silver coin, which appears to have been a rara avis. After the ships had been thoroughly ransacked and plundered they were dispatched as prizes to this to port, but even more trials undergo ; all the ships stores then they had having been stolen, these were replaced by a j very small quantity of the worst description and with no water, and thus they had to iind their way here, no captain or crew being allowed to go in his own vessel ; but did the unfortunate captains and passengers think at that series would end on arrival the capital of their mitliis, civilized Republic? communication was added as a refinement of barbarity. But will the Danish and Dutch authorities quietly see their ships and their subjects treated in this manner? They must answer for themselves. So much for the exploits of the Dominicans afloat ! Santana has fallen at last It was taken by assault on the dial inst., ami the. defeated General Parmantier, who escaped alone to this city without having been able to realize his fond project of blowing himself up before lie allowed bis port to be taken, has been appointed Commander-in-Chief of the defence ,,f this city. I spoke to my brave steed, addressing him by name ; I urged him with hands and knees ; only at intervals did I inflict the cruel steel upon his ribs. I soon perceived that he was flagging ; I perceived it with increased apprehension for the result, lie had worn his saddle too long on the day before, and the wet weary night had jaded him. Ho had been overwrought, and I felt his weariness, as he galloped with feebler stroke. The prairie-steed must have been fresh in comparison. But life and death were upon the issue. Her life þÿ perhaps my own. I cared not to survivo her. She must be saved. The spur must bo plied without remorse : the steed must be overtaken, even if Moro should die ! It was a rolling prairie over which the chase ! led þÿ a surface that undulated like the billows of the ocean. We galloped transversely to the direction of the þÿ swells, that rose one after the other in rapid succession. Perhaps the rapidity with which wc were crossing them brought them nearer to each other. To me there appeared no level ground between these land-billows. Up hill and down hill in quick alternation was the manner of our progress þÿ a severe trial upon the girths þÿ a hard killing gallop for my poor horse. But life and death were upon the issue, and the spur must be plied without remorse.

A long cruel gallop þÿ would it never come to an end ? would the steed never tire ? would ho never stop ? Surely in time he must become weary ? Surely Moro was his equal in strength as in speed ? þÿ superior to him iu both ? Ah! the prairie-horse possessed a double advantage þÿ he had started fresh þÿ he was on his native ground. I kept my eyes fixed upon him ; not for one moment did I withdraw my glance. A mysterious apprehension was upon me; 1 feared to look around, lest he should disappear. The souvenirs of the former chase still haunted me; weird remembrances clung to my spirit. I was once more in the region of the supernatural. 1 looked neither to the right nor left, but straight before me þÿ straight at the object of my pursuit, and the distance that lay between us. This last 1 continuously scanned, now with fresh hope, and now again with doubt. It seemed to vary with the ground. At one time, 1 was nearer, as the descending slope gave me the i there was none. Silent advantage; but the moment after, the steep declivity retarded the speed of my horse, and increased the intervening distance. It was with joy I crossed the last swell of the rolling prairie, and beheld a level plain stretch- I my rash haste, I might yet have been upon the ing before us. It was with joy I perceived that ! trail þÿ upon the new ground I was rapidly gaining upon the steed ! And rapidly I continued to gain upon him, until scarcely three hundred yards were between us. So near was 1, that I could trace the out-

lines of her form þÿ her prostrate limbs þÿ still lashed to the croup þÿ her garments loose and torn þÿ her ankles þÿ her long dark hair dishevelled and trailing to the ground þÿ even her pallid cheek I could perceive, as at intervals tile steed tossed back his head to utter his wild taunting neigh. 1 was near enough to be heard. I shouted in my loudest voice ; I called her by name. I kept my eyes upon her, and with throbbing anxiety listened for a response. I fancied that her head was raised, as though she understood and would have answered me. I could hear no voice, but her feeble cry might have been drowned by the clatter of the hooves. Again I called aloud þÿ again and again pronouncing her namo. Surely I heard a cry ; surely her head was raised from the withers of the horse. I could not be mistaken. þÿ Thank Heaven, she lives þÿ! I had scarcely uttered the prayer, when 1 felt my steed yield beneath mo as though he was sinking into the bosom of the, earth. I was hurled out of the saddle, and flung head-foremost upon the plain. But as I headed my horse once more toward the chase, the white steed and his rider had passed out of sight. CHAPTER LXVI. LOST IN A CHAPPARAL. I was chagrined, frantic, and despairing, but not surprised. This time there was no mystery about the disappearance of the steed ; the chap- j paral explained it. Though I no longer saw him, he was yet within hearing. His footfall on the firm ground, the occasional snapping of a dead stick, the whisk of the recoiling branches, all reached my ears as I was remounting. These sounds guided me, aud without staying to follow his tracks, I dashed forward to the edge of the chapparal þÿ at the point nearest to where I heard him moving4 I did not pause to look for an opening, but heading iu the direction whence came the sounds, 1 spurred forward into the thicket. Breasting the bushe s that reached around his neck, or bounding over them, my brave horse pressed on ; but he had not goue three lengths of himself before I recognised the imprudence of the course I was pursuing : 1 now saw I should have followed the tracks. I no longer heard the movements of the steed þÿ neither toot-stroke, nor snapping sticks, nor breaking branches. The noise made by my own horse, amid the crackling acacias, drowned every other sound; and so long as I kept in motion, 1 moved with uncertainty. It was ouly when 1

made stop that 1 could again hear the ehasc struggling through the thicket ; þÿ sounds were faint aud far distant growing still but now the fainter as l listened. Once more I urged forward my horse, heading him almost at random ; but I had not advanced a hundred paces, before the misery of uncertainty again impelled me to halt. This time 1 listened and heard nothing þÿ not even the recoil of a bough. 'The steed had either stopped, and was standing silent, or, what was more probable, had gained so far in advance 1 of me that his hoof-stroke was out of hearing. Half frautic, augered at myself, too much excited for cool reflection, I lanced the sides of my horse, aud galloped madly through the | thicket. 1 rode several hundred yards before drawing bridle, in a sort of desperate hope I might ouee more bring myself within earshot of the chase. Again I halted to listen. My recklessness proved of no avail. To recover the trace of him, I made several casts across the thicket. 1 rode first in one direction, then in another, but all to no purpose. 1 could find neither hoof-track nor broken branch. I next bethought me of returning to the open prairie, there retaking the trail, and following it thence. This was clearly the wisest, in fact, the only course in which there was reason. Lost in the chapparal þÿ that parched and hideous jungle, where every plant that carries a thorn seemed to have place. Around grew acacias, minosat, gliditschiat, robimot, a/garobia

Through this horrid thicket 1 had not passed unscathed ; my garments were already torn, my limbs were bleeding. My þÿlimbs and hers ? We have much pleasure in announcing the arrival in this Island of Baron de Fleur, the celebrated Pianist and Composer. THE WAR-TRAIL. A ROMANCE. in CAPTAIN MAY NT. REID CHAPTER LX VII. KNCOl'NTUR WITH JAVAI.I. It was u question whether they would follow mine, or that of the steed. This bad not occurred to me before, and 1 paused to consider it. If thu former, then was I wrong in moving onward, as I should ouly be going from them, and leading them in a longer search. Already had 1 given them a knot to unravel, my devious path forming a labyrinthine maze. It was more than probable they would follow me þÿ ill the belief that I bad some reason for diviatiug from the trail of the steed, perhaps for the purpose of heading or intercepting him. This conjecture decided me þÿagai >i> advancing further þÿ at least until some time should elapse, enough to allow them to come up with me. Out of compassion for my hard-breathing horse, 1 dismounted At intervals, I shouted aloud, and fired shots from my pistols: after each I listened; but neither shot nor shout reached mo in reply. They must be distant indeed, not to hear the report of fire-arms ; for had they heard tin >n, they would have been certain to make answer in a similar manner. All of them carried rifles and pistols. 1 began to think it was tune they should have reached me. Again I fired several shots; but. as before, echo was the only reply Perhaps they had not followed me : perhaps they had kept on upon the trail of the steed, and it might lead them far away, beyond hearing o( the reports t perhaps there was not yet time for them to have arrived ? While thus conjecturing, my ears were assail-

ed by the screeching of birds at some distance off. I recognised the harsh notes of the jay, mingling with the chatter of the red cardinal. From the tones, 1 know that these birds were excited by the presence of some animal. Perhaps they were defending their nests against tlm black snake or the crotalus. It might be my followers ap; roach ing ? it might he the steed þÿ like me, still wandering in the cliapparal ? I sprang to my saddle to get a better view, and gazed over the tops of the trees. Guided by the voices of the birds, 1 soon discovered the scene of the commotion. At some distance off. I saw both jays and cardinals fluttering among the branches, evidently excited by something on the ground bcueath them. At the same time l heard strange noises, far louder than the voices of the birds, hut could not tell what was causing then). My spirits sank, for 1 knew they could not he produced either by my comrades or the steed. It was not far, and 1 determined to satisfy myself as to wliat was causing such a commotion in this hitherto silent place. I rode towards the spot, as fast as my horse could make way through the hushes. I was soon satisfied Coming out on the edge of a little glade. 1 became spectator to a strnngc scene þÿ a battle between t lie red cougar and a hand of /arah The fierce little boars were ' þÿringing the. panther, who was fighting desperately in their midst. Several of them lay upon the grournl. struck senseless or dead, by thu stroug paws of the huge cat ; hut the others, nothing daunted,

had completely surrounded their enemy and were hounding upon him with open mouths, wounding him with their sharp shining tusks. The scene aroused my hunter instincts, and suddenly unslinging my rifle, I set my eye to the sights. I had no hesitation about the selection of my mark þÿ the panther, by all means þÿ and drawing trigger, I sent my bullet through the þÿcreature skull, s at ouee stretching him out in the midst of his assailants. Three seconds had not elapsed, before 1 had reason to regret the choice I had made of a victim. I should have let the cougar alouv, and cither held my fire, or directed it upon one of his urchin-like enemies; for the moment, he was hors de combat , his assailants became mine þÿ transferring 1 þÿsurround to my horse and myself, with all the savage fierceness they had just exhibited towards the panther ! I had no means of punishing the ungrateful brutes. They had not given me time to reload

my riflo before commencing the attack, and my pistols were both empty. My horse, startled by the unexpected assault, as well as by the strange creatures that were making it, snorted and plunged wildly over the grouud ; but go where he would, a score of the ferocious brutes followed, springing against his sides, and scoring his shanks with their terrible tusks. Well for me I was able to keep the saddle ; had been thrown from it at that moment, I should certainly have been torn to pieces. I saw no hope of safety but in flight, and spurring ray horse, I gave him full rein. Alas! through that tangled thicket the jav.ali could go as fast as ho ; and after galloping a hundred yards or so, I perceived the whole flock still around me, leaping as fiercely as ever around the limbs of my steed. The result might have proved awkward enough ; but at that moment I heard voices, and saw mounted men breaking through the underwood. They were Stanfield, Quackenboss, and the rest of the rangers. In another second they were on the ground ; and their revolvers, playing rapidly, soon thinned the ranks of the javali, and caused the survivors to retreat grunting and screaming into the thicket. CHAPTER LXVIII. THE WOODS ON FIRE ? The trappers were not among those who had rescued me þÿ where were they ? The others made answer, though I already guessed what they had to tell. Rube and Garey had followed the tracks of the steed, leaving the rangers to come after me. I was pleasod with the ready intelligence of

my comrades: they had acted exactly as they should have done. I was myself found, and I no longer entertained any apprehension that the trail would be lost. By this time, the trappers must be far upon it ; more than an hour had elapsed siuce they and the others had parted company. My zigzag path had cost my followers many a bewildering pause. But they had not ridden recklessly as 1, and could find their way back. As it was impossible to tell in what direction Rube and Garcy had gone, this course was the best to bo followed; and under the guidance of Stanfield, an expert woodsman, wc commenced returning to the prairie. It was not necessary to follow back our own crooked trail The Keutuckian had noted the þÿ þÿlay of the chapparal, and led us out of its labyrinths by an almost direct path. On reaching the open prairie, we made no halt ; but upon the tracks of Rube, Garcy, and the steed, once more entered the chapparal. Wc had no difficulty about our course ; it was plainly traced out for us ; the trappers had þÿ blazed it. In most places, the tracks of the three horses were sufficient indices of the route ; but there were stretches where the ground was stony, and upon the parched arid herbage, even the shod hoof left no visible mark. In such places, a branch of acacia broken and pendulous, the bent flower-stem of an aloe or the succulent leaves of the cactus slashed with a sharp knife, were conspicuous and unmistakable signs ; and by the guidance of these we made rapid advance.

Wo must have gone much faster than the trackers themselves þÿ for notwithstanding the freshness of the trail, there were dry spots and patches of cut rock over which it passed, and where it must have cost both time and keen perception to trace it. As we were travelling so much more rapidly than Rube and Garey could have done, I looked forward to our soon overtaking them ; with eager anticipation, I looked forward. Surely by this time they must have come in sight of the steed ? þÿ perhaps captured him ? 0 joyous anticipation ! Or would they return with a different tale ? Though hastening on after the trackers, there were moments when I feared to overtake them þÿ moments when I dreaded to hear their talc ! The Independance JJe/pe publishes the following as an accurate account of what took place in the first three sittings of. the Paris Confe- j rcnces : þÿ The fust bitting was altogether devoted to the necessary formalities. In the second, the question of the reorganisation of the Danubiau

Principalities was at once taken up. The discussion was opened by the French plenipotentiary distinctly proposing the union in such a way that the institution of two hospodars should be preserved, hut that there should be only one and the same constitution, and one ! and the same Legislative Senate for both Principalities. In this exposition Count Walewski i was interrupted bv the English plenipotentiary, j Lord Cowley, who proposed that a certain or- ; dec ought to be observed in the discussion of j the different schemas, and that the initiative unqii. stiouably belonged to Turkey, after which the neighbouring States, Austria and Russia, in this order could claim to be heard, while I France. Great Britain, Prussia, and Sardinia would conclude the discussion in their alphabetical order. This proposition was supported bv the Austrian plenipotentiary, and unani- \ mouslv adopted. .But the Turkish plenipotentiary, Fuad I'acha, being thus called upon to speak first, had nothing to say, and confined himself to a general assertion that Turkey wished tlio affair regulated to the satisfaction I and with the consent of all the Governments represented. The plenipotentiaries of Russia and Austria, next called upon to speak, had likewise nothing to say, and it seemed that a general feeling of uneasiness led to an early adjournment of the sitting. At the next sitting, Count Walewski, thinking himself now entitled t<> speak, commenced again to expound the very succinct and detailed proposition of

Franco, when the English plenipotentiary interrupted him again, apd reminded the Conference that the initiative belonged to Fuad Pacha But Fuad Pacha this time positively declared that his instructions did not allow him to make any distinct proposition to the Conference, and that his only business was to oppose any proposition including the project of union The Austrian plenipotentiary, whose turn then came, proposed to discuss the organio rcgula tions lor the two Principalities. The Russian and the English plenipotentiaries had no propositions to make. The Prussian plenipotentiary was likewise without instructions, and be proposed to discuss first international law regulating the relations between the Sultan and the Principalities It became then evident hat the state of the instructions permitted no useful discussion at all, and the Conference resolved to adjourn till the. 10th, when each plenipotentiary promised to be furnished with

Tg & Bi a t ft V! f: $ new instructions. The Conference refused to accept Count þÿWalewski s as well as Herr vott þÿHubner propositions s to protocol ; and, in fact, the first three sittings were thus entirely thrown away. Of the sittings which followed, nothing as yet is known with certainty, except that the French project after two þÿdays discussion, was lost on the 14th, most probably without the question having been put to the vote The further meetings of the Conferences are postponed in consequence of the indisposition of Fuad Effeudi. The Const it utionnel is furious at Lord Mal- i þÿmesbury sspeech about the introduction of 1 negroes into French colonies. In an article signed by M. Renee, it commences its demonstration that France is not carrying on the I slave-trade under false pretences, with a great deal of abuse of England for her cruelty in India aud her misgovernment of Ireland- After having exhausted these extraneou:, sub jects, it dwells on þÿ the generosity and '.he noble sentiment of glory which is revealed iu every page of French þÿhistory, and draws a pretty sketch of nations and governments awaiting from this side of the Rhiue, þÿ not only the signal of a progress in moral order, but | also the heroical aud disinterested devotion I which carries that progress into þÿexecution. ! At length condescending to come to the point, the Constitutionnel denies in the following terms the truth of the statement made by the Earl of Malmesbury : þÿ þÿ The pretended slaves on board the Regina Cceli were not slaves; they

were men who had been free for a loug time past; they were citizens of two republics, exported from the United States to Liberia, who had freely contracted engagements for our colonies, and who had no other motive in revolting, than thirst of blood and love of i pillage. Need we add that it is false, entirely false, that irons or chains are to bo found on board our vessels employed in the emigration trade ? It is a pure invention. Everybody is aware that recruiting of Africans is effected under the active and able surveillance of French cruisers, under the immediate control of the administration, which places an agent on | board every vessel employed, and under the eyes of the surgeon who has a responsibility to protect. The positive accusations made in the House of Lords were therefore void of all pretext as of all þÿfoundation. ! The Patrie is much more dignified and the matter of the Regina Cadi it says : þÿ reasonable on this subject. With reference to þÿ His lordship was pleased to say that this vessel, the crew of which was horribly massacred, had no emigrants on board, but a cargo of slaves ; and that the system of emigration, by which the Freuch Government endeavours to introduce free blacks into its colonies, is nought but | a renewal of the slave-trade. We must protest against these assertions. It may be that the system chosen by our Government is defective; this is generally the fate of most undertakings at their outset ; but it would be sovereignly ! unjust to suspect the intentions of France.

France has no intention of returning to slavery, , which she has abolished ; she has only sought tlio means of supplying her colonies with tree labourers. Should this syAcm encourage abuses, France will employ all her zeal in preventing them ; should these abuses prove ' inseparable from the system, she will abandon the system itself with the same frankness with which she had adopted þÿit. A worse appetite than hunger assailed my companions, and I felt it with the rest þÿ it was thirst: for hours all had been suffering from it; the long hard ride had brought it on, aud now the smoke aud the dry hot atmosphere increased the appetite till it had grown agonising, almost unendurable. In the centre of a largo black screen there is a space filled with a square of ground glass, upon which, by some light managed behind the screen, is thrown a magnified photographic image representing a landscape, a portrait, or any other object. When looked at without the help of any optical instrument the picture is seen in perfect relief as when wc look at two differant pictures through a stereoscope. It is not tiecessarv to be at a fixed distance from the picture : it may he examined as well at w ith feet as at one foot, as an ordinary picture, teu out the least fatigue to the eyes. Although

considerably enlarged by the instrument itself, the picture may be magnified still more by using large convex lensi-s ; and two or three persons at once can examine it with the greatest ease. The illusion of relief docs not take place if the image is received on paper. YVhen the medium is ground gin-, the rays refracted by the various points of the lens upon that sur face are only visible when they are incident in a line coinciding w ith the optic axis. So that the rays emerging from the ground glass, and entering the right eye, are only those which are refracted obliquely in the same direction, by the left side of the object-glass: and those entering the left eye are only those which are refracted by the right side of the object-glass ; consequently, both eyes have n different view and perspective of the object represented on the ground glass, and the single image is. in ; point of fact, the result of two images, eacl only visible to one eye. INTERESTING FROM NICARAGUA. San Juan pel Norir, May 4, 1858. This little town, for the last fifteen days, has been the theatre of some very stormy events, of which 1 give you herewith a short but accurate account. On the 17th o( April Colonel Kinney, with six other persons, arrived here and made an attempt to overthrow the local government. The Colonel was some time ago the owner of a house here, which was subsequently mortgaged to Wood and Son. On the Colonel's departure about eight months since, he appointed Mr B Mooney his agent, aud the mortgage

having fallen due, it was foreclosed and the pro perty put up to auction ; Wood & Son bought it in for some eleven hundred dollars, and not being able to let it, the house was closed up. The Colonel's first act on landing was to find out from his old friends how matters stood, and then after dark he effected an entrance on the premises and took forcible possession of the property, setting at defiance the authorities of the town. I he next day being Sunday nothing was done. On Monday Mr. Cullin, the Purser of the United States sloop Jamestown, exerted himself with both parties to have the matter left to arbitration, which was agreed to ; three arbitrators were named, bonds were entered into to abide by their decision, and one week from date allowed for them to give in their verdict. On the 25th, Kinney and his associates prepared a Niearaguan Flag, aud on Sunday about midday proceeded to where the Mosquito Flag was hoisted, pulled it down, and raised the Nicaraguan ensign in its place, lo this act the town authorities offered no opposition. The Colonel's next act was to address a letter to the Mayor, of which the following is a correct cony : (No. 1.) San Juan del Norte, Nicaragua. April 25, 1858. To Julius Wolff, Esq. Dear Sir, þÿ The" people of San Juan del Norte having called upon me to assume the power, protem , desire me to notify you that, owing to the late treaty between the United States and Nicaragua, the former government and your office are annulled from this time
forth.

(Signed) II L. Kinney Shortly after sending this document to the Mayor, Colonel Kinney or i ui < some of his party to ask Mr. Wolff to come down, which the latter refused to do. Kinney then ordered a warrant to he issued for his arrest, of which 1 send a copy. (No. 2) San Juan Del Norte, April 25, 1S5S. To Captain Pool, Sir, þÿ 1 hereby order you to proceed, and bring before ine at the guard house, by order of Colonel Kinney, Julius Wolff, Esq., former Mayor of this City. (Signed) G. 11. Glideon. Armed with this document, Pool went to the Mayor and demanded his surrender, hut the Mayor again refused ; Pool then returned for fresh instructions, and received orders to take the Mayor dead or alive. Accompanied bv tour or five men, Pool went again to the Mayor's Tesidenco which he found closed against him ; alter many threats of p illing down the house, one of Pool's men asked for few moments private conversation with the Mayor; pledging his word that no one else of the party should euter the house ; this was granted, but no seized the key, pitched opened sooner was the door it out the window and than the party then made Mr. Wolff prisoner. On being brought to the guard house, where a large crowd had collected, the Mayor asked Colonel Kinney the reason why he was thus treated, to which the Colonel replied that he wished to inform him officially of what had taken place, that the flag hart been changed, the old government deposed, and his (Kinney's) substituted. The Mayor then asked ti e peo-

ple if they wished him to resign, to which there was a general cry of "no, no;" the Mayor then asked Kinney by what authority he dared to act as he. had done and declared his intention not to resign. ( Loud cheers from the citizens.) Kinney replied that he acted by authority of Captain Kennedy of the United States frigate Jamestown, and that if the Mayor interfered with the Hag the Captain would call him to account for it þÿ this report had been circulated for two days previous and was generally credited þÿ the Mayor on hearing this said that if Kinney was hacked by the Captain of the man-of-war he could not resist, but expressed .a wish to have an interview with Captain Kennedy. Whilst all this was going on Mr. Paten, Her British Majesty's Consul, went on hoard the Jamestown, the United States Commercial Agent was sent for and in about an hour both of these gentlemen accompanied by Capt. Kennedy, came on shore and had an interview of two hours with Colonel Kinney. After this was over. Mr. Paten wished to present the Mayor

to the Captain, but the latter refused, on the grounds that he did not acknowledge his office. At the residence of the United States Commercial Agent, Captain Kennedy was informed how Kinney had made use of his name, whereupon he stated that such was not the case, and that he never made a remark that could lead to Kinney's using his name. After this the Captain went on board, and as it was late, nothing more transpired that night. The next day, a meeting of citizens was held at the Mayor's house, and whilst it was in conclave, Kinney sent an order to deliver up to him the cannon belonging to the Town, this was replied to by an order from the Mayor for Kinney's arrest, and just as the marshal and a large body of citizens were about to put it in force, five of the Jamestown' s cutters, filled with armed marines, were observed pulling towards the shore. þÿ The citizens then proceeded to the British Consul's to await the course of events, and were engaged in making a protest, when Captain Kennedy joined them On hearing of Kinney's acts, and how his name had been made use of, the Captain declared that it was done without his permission or approval. þÿ He then read the protest, (having at first refused to do so) and finding Kinney in the wrong, he said he only wanted to prevent bloodshed. After this, lie (the Captain ) visited the United States Commercial Agent, and then had a long interview with Kinney. About S o'clock be sent a letter to the Mayor, stating that ho would not interfere to prevent Kinney's arrest,

and that he only wished to prevent bloodshed. Thus ended the day's proceedings Next morning a big crowd collected to aid the authorities in arresting Kinney. At first he threatened to resent, but at length ,e agreed to surrender to the Americans, and was taken to the guard house Captain Kennedy soon after came on shore, when after much discussion the following document was drawn up and signed " We the undersigned agree and pledge our- by the parties. selves jointly and severally to accept the asylum tendered us by Captain Kennedy, of the United States ship-of-war Jamestown, and that he will this day proceed on board of the said ship, and remain there without coming on shore to Greytown, until we can avail ourselves of the earliest opportunity of leaving by bung > or other conveyance for the interior of the country ; and we pledge ourselves jointly and severally that we will not return to this town, except with peaceable and friendly intention to the local authorities and all the residents thereof. This agreement lias been concluded by the intervention of Capt. Kennedy, Lieut. C. G. McCauly, United States Marine Corps, of the United State ship-of-war Jamestown, and Julius Wolff, Mayor of the town, aud has been accepted by the undersigned in good faith, to which we solemnly pledge ourselves without equivocation or reserve. Signed in duplicate at Greytown or San Juan del Norte April 27, 1858 In the preseuce of C. H. Kennedy, Commander United States ship Jamestown, C. G.

U SU GRENADA Grenada papers ( the Chronicle) by the Conway , this morning, inform us of the arrival of Lieut. -Colonel Ready, to assume the Government of the Colony during the absence of Mr Kortwright, the Lieut -Governor, and to super sede the President, Mr. Checkley, who sue ceeded to the Administration of Affairs the, departure of Mr. Kortwright from the I J. and who has several times before carried the Government satisfactorily in the absence of the Lieut. -Governor ; a change which is by no means agreeable to the inhabitants of the Island, who complain of the appointment of Lieut. -Colonel Ready over the head of Mr. Checkley, as an innovation to upon tution. And really it seems us a just ground their Constiof complaint, which might become ours tomorrow ; for supposing the absence of Mr. Iliucks, arising either temporarily or permanently, why should Colonel Ready, or any other person nominated by the Governor, succeed to the Administration of affairs, to the exclusion of the President of the Council. We cannot agree to the now doctrine of the Globe, that there is no such thing as abstract rights in the Constitution of these Colonies. Next we shall be told there is no such thing as a Constitution. We have a Constitution ; let us abide by its invariable customs ; if it becomes expedient to change them, to meet the changes of society, let such changes be introduced openly, and be made authoritatively, with the sanction of the Legislature, and not underhandedly and indirectly, by settiug up irregular

This Island, containing a population of 13,000 souls and ranking high in the commercial world, exhibits in regard to its judicial administration a striking contrast to other places. The offices of Police Magistrate, civil, criminal, and military Judge, Recorder, Sheriff and Auctioneer in Chief are united in one person ; while another individual holds the situation of Notary and Judge of the Court of Insolvency and Estates of Intestates. The whole judicial powvr is thus wielded by two officials. The result is said to he that the Courts of Justice are conducted in strict conformity with the rules of " the circumlocution Pepartinont,'' redtapism the order of the day. Were the wheel of

Justice only clogged by ' the laws delay,'' it would be to the inhabitants a passable state of things. But as the Police Magistrate is Coroner, Inquisitor, Judj and Sheriff in all cases, the " plurality" is j ("judicial and dangerous i i the extreme to the welfare and liberty of the ci. reus It is in the power of the Magistrate to imprison any person on mere suspicion, during pleasure, without redress. The prisoner, v ho is not allowed Council, until placed on his trial, and if the crime is grave is examined by the Magistrate only , within closed doors. The examination with few exceptional cases, is, of necessity, (in a community where all other languages are spoken but Danish, except an ong the officials,) carried on in a language which it is a matter of impossibility that the Magistrate can thoroughly understand. With regard to the Mutes or Police witnesses, who always are disbanded soldiers, ali foreign languages are entirely above their comprehension. It may be inferred that the prisoner's innocence must be very palpable for him to hope for an acquittal from the man who has committed and judges him. This way of dispensing justice is more objectionable as this official is not selected among the Barristers or Serjeants, but often young men from college are appointed to fill such important offices. The prisoner is reliiaudeU from time to time ad infinitum ; for the Magistmtc may state that his other functions prevent him from bringing the investigation or case to an end, and thus the hapless wight of a

prisoner sutlers the torture of solitaiy confinement during many months ; in particular as it would appear, that it is left to the caprice of the Magistrate, whether he will accept bail for any offence. Iu all civil cases the Magistrate may likewise defer giving judgment, on the plea of this multifarious occupation. It is said that some years ago the above enumerated offices were filled by four officials, but for economical purposes the offices are now made to suit the men but not the men the offices. It may cause surprise that such a state of things is tolerated in a community containing many men ot intelligence, wealth and influence But there is no liberty of the Press j it is at the option of the Police Magistrate as Censor to erase the most inoffensive article in the proof sheet of the only newspaper published in the Island. There is no local legislative Assembly to fix the fares and rates and reform the laws or to control the administration of justice. However, it is rumoured that a change is at hand. A young Jurist, lately from the " Fatherland," is to assume the offices of civil, cr minal, and military Judge, Recorder, Sheriff, Auctioneer, Notary and Judge of the Court of B.uikru its and Intestates. The Police Magistracy to be retained by that present Incumbent who, although peculiarly suited to attend to tiie "cleanness and sweepings of streets and rattles," as a Judge lias been found lame. What will be gained by the change is bidden in futurity ; but it is certain that the new functionary will be so saddled

and hampered with the business of the whole judicial department, except one branch, that his task will lie a difficult one to satisfy the requirements of the community. Changes are seldom reform. The exception is the Police Court. Surely, if any department requires reformity, this does. The Magistrate decides various civil cases. In petty criminal cast's lie inflicts punishment as high as six months' hard labor No lawyers are admitted at this Court. In private civil suits, the Police Magistrate acts as Lawyer to both plaintiff and defendant and Judge to boot ! He is Lawyer for the Crown in petty criminal prosecutions and Judge! Persons are as it were tried and condemned without Judge or þÿJury; they are, however, well peppered. The public are likewise excluded at all times, and justice is summarily executed. Cyrus Mills, a British subject, hut a resident married man, and another man are challenged by a Policeman for their porter-passes, which they answer are at home, as they do nol intend to work to-day. They are ordered up to the Office by the Policeman, " who takes hold of tho other. Mills for observing you need not hold the man, he will not run away," is flogged by order of the Magistrate, and, for asking the reason why, is refiogged on the spot and sent to public labour with an iron spur on his leg. A gentleman «l English parentage, is arrested for presumed participation in the late Catholic riots. On ins examination a nafcr, a drunkard, and a bawd appear as witnesses against him. He objects against

tlicm ; hut their evidences arc taken. He desires that two French masters of vessels, and two respectable inhabitants, who were present at the riot as spectators, should be cited as witnesses, hut his request is rejected. He was, h' wever, condemned on the evidence of the forementioned witnesses! To note similar cases would exceed the extent of our present journal, hut in a future number we shall jot down some more; for Justice here is wide awake þÿ most awfully, and offers rich matter for the Travellers notice C. The pleasant excitement caused by my visit to niy old comrades was soon over ; and having nothing to do but lounge about my tent, I bod- came again the victim of the same painful beings. I could not shake them off. Subtile and mysterious is the spirit-world within us ; certainly docs it seem to have prescience of the future. Is it an electric chain connecting what is, with what is to be I Or there second-sight of instinct? Certainly is it the are times when something within whispers a warning, as, in the physical world, God's wild creatures arc warned from without of the earthquake and the storm. How often do wo experience the realisation of portentous dreams ? Why should not the waking soul have also its moments oi clairvoyance ? As I lay stretched upon my leathern catre, I gave way to such reflections. 1 soon succeeded in reasoning myself into a full belief in foretionately strengthened. knowledge ; and my apprehensions were propor- a Hut 1 had conceived design, and the prospect of putting it in execution somewhat relieved me from the heaviness I had hitherto felt. My new project was to take a score of my best men, to ride back the road we had come, place the party in ambush near the hacienda, while I aloDe should enter the house, and further urge the counsels I had committed to writing. If I should find that these had been already followed, so much the better þÿ I should be assured,

and return content ; but I felt almost certain that Don Ramon had rejected them. At all events, I was determined to know the truth þÿ determined, moreover, to gratify my longing for one more interview with my beloved. I had warned the men and fixed the hour þÿ as soon as it was dark enough to conceal our departure from the camp. 1 had two reasons for not starting earlier þÿ first, because I did not wish this private scouting to be known at head-quarters. It is true that in such matters wc rangers had the advantage of regular troops. Though belonging to the division, our duty was usually detached from it, and we were rarely ' missed' when absent. There was thus a sort of pleasant independence in my command, which I for one fully appreciated. For all that, I did uot desire the whole world to know of an expedition like the one projected. My second motive for going in the night was simple prudence. I dared not take thr whole of my command along with tue without permission from above. The absence of the corps without leave would certainly be noticed, even were it but for a few hours ; and with the smaller party I intended to take, caution would bo requisite. Should we move along the road before it was deserted, seme swift messenger might carry the tidings en avant , and get us into trouble. I designed to start at the earliest hour of darkness, so that might I not alarm the hacienda by a midnight visit. An hour and a half of constant riding would bring me to its gate. At the last moment of twilight wc were in

our saddles ; and rode silently into the chapparal that skirted our camp. After filing for some distance through a narrow path, we debouched upon the up-river road þÿ the samo that conducted to the ranclioria. The trappers, Rube and Garcy, acting as scouts, went forward in the advance. They were on foot þÿ their horses romaining behind with the party. It was a mode of march I had adopted after some experience in bush-fighting. The scouts of a marching force should always go on foot, whether the main body be dragoons or infantry. In this manner they can take advantage of the ground ; and by keeping under cover of the timber, are enabled to reconnoitre the angles of the road in a much safer way than when on horseback. The great danger to a scout þÿ and consequently to the party for which he is acting þÿ lies in his being first seen, and the risk is greater when he cover be drawn under is mounted. The horse cannot without an effort ; and the sound of the hoof may be heard ; whereas in nine cases out of ten, a mau on foot þÿ that is

Of course the scout should never advance beyond the possibility of retreating upon the party he is guiding. With full confidence in the men who had been sent forward, we rode on timing our pace, so as not to overtake them. Now and then we caught a glimpse of them, at the further end of a long stretch, skirting the bushes, or stooping behind the cover, to reconnoitre the road in advance. To our chagrin, it was clear moon-light, and we could distinguish their forms at a great distance. We should much have preferred darker-night. a The road wc were travelling upon was entirely without habitations ; most of it ran through light stead. chapparal forest, with neither stood One solitary rancho clearing nor home- at about equal distances between the town and the rancheria and liar sobriquet was known among the rangers by the fami- of the ' half-way house ' It was a poor hovel of yucca, with a small patch around that had once grown yams, chile-pepper, and a stock of maize for whoever had inhabited it ; but its occupants had long since disappeared þÿ the prowling soldier-robber from the camp had paid it many a visit, and its household gods lay broken upon the hearth. The tortilla stone and comal, red earthen ollas, calabash cups, bedsteads and benches of the cana vaquera, a whirligig spindle, an old stringle8s jarana or bandolon, with other like effects, lay in fragments upon the floor.

Mingling with these were cheap that prints, of saints and Saviour, coloured wood- had been leaves dragged from the walls, and with the in torn of an old Spanish misa, trampled dust and dishonour. I paint this tableau of ruiu, not that it was in any way connected with the events of our narrative, but that it had strangely affected me. On the day before, as we rode past, 1 had halted a moment by the littlo rancho, and contemplated the scene with a feeling of melancholy that amounted almost to sadness. Littlo thought I that a still sadder spectacle awaited me in that same spot. We had approached within less than half a mile of the rancho, when a strange medley of sounds reached our cars. Human voices they were, and borne upon the light breeze wc could distinguish them to be the voices of women. Occasionally harsher tones were heard mingling in the murmur, but most of them had the sott rich intonation that distinguishes the female voice. Wc all drew bridle, and listened. The sounds continued in the same confused chorus, but there was neither song nor joy in the accents. On the contrary, the night-wind carried upon its wings the voices ot 'lamentation and wailing.' ' There are women in trouble,' remarked one of my followers in a loud suggestive tone. The remark caused all ot us simultaneously to ply the spur, and ride forward Before wc had galloped a dozen lengths, a man appeared coming from the opposite direction, and advancing rapidly up the middle ot the road. We saw it was the scout Garey ; and, once

more reining up, we awaited his approach. 1 was at the head of the little troop, and as the trapper drew near, I could see his face lull under the light of the moon. Its expression was ominous of evil tidings. He spoke not until he had laid his hand upon the pommel my of saddle, and then only in a subdued and saddened tone. His words were : 'Tliar's ugly news, capt'n.' O that terrible foreboding! 'News? þÿ ill news ?' I stammered out; 'what, for Heaven's sake ? þÿ speak, Garey!' ' They've been playin' the devil at the ranchcrie. Them ruffins hez behaved wuss than Injuns would a done. But come lorrard, capt'n, an see for yurself. The wcemen are clost by hyar at the shanty. Rube's a tryin' to pacify them, poor critters.' 0 that terrible foreboding ! 1 made no response to Garey 's last speech, but rode forward as fast as my horse could carry me- A brace of minutes brought mc up to the rancho, and there I beheld a spectacle that caused j town the blood to curdle in my veins.

From the Weekly Despatch, Man 23, 1858.) INDIA. The Indian news is not cheerful. It is plain that we have a very ungrateful task before us, the putting down of a guerilla war in a seasou which the natives can endure, but which strikes our soldiery down with sheer exhaustion. British pluck surmounts all ; but this contest with enemies who evade battle and can march 40 miles a day to our 20, will try it. Many of the talootcdars of Oude appear to be hastening to Mr. Montgomery, the new commissioner, to secure the mercy tendered in the Proclamation ; though, by another account, some chieftains are þÿ ing to fight out the quarrel to the death doubt- preparless those hopelessly compromised by their former acts. Mr. Montgomery is confessedly " the right man in the right place," a circumstance far too fortunate to be overlooked in these times of difficulty.

FRANCE. Political affairs are almost eclipsed in interest by what may fairly be called an organised attempt on the part ol a number of officers of the army to kill a literary man, under the pretence of a duel, which was fought on Friday in the Bois de Vesinay, near St. Germain. 51. Henry do Penc, a well-known literary man. who for some time wrote the feuilleton in the Nord of Brussels which was signed "Nemo,'' and who has lately written in the Paris Figaro under the same signature, made some playful remarks in a recent article about the sub-lieutenauts of the army. The article gave an account of a ball at M. Gousberg's, a Russian merchant, who is dazzling Paris with the dispassage : play of his þÿ " A decided improvement following wealth, and contained the ' We looked in vain in the salons of M. and Mdtne. Gousbcrg for the inevitable sub-lieutenant that haunts the festive reunions of obscure fashionables. The said sub-lieutenant, in full uniform if you please, lacerating lace uniforms with his spurs, operating a razzia on the refreshments, is the plague þÿ the inevitable plague þÿ of newborn salons, lie is asked once, but never makes a second appearance. As soon as the salons in question have cut their teeth, they get rid of the unwelcome guest." This article gave offence in a mess-room at St. Germain, and in his weekly article of Sunday the 9th inst., " Nemo" observed that he had received a very coarse letter from a person who signed himself " A Sub- Lieutenant," and who talked

a great deal more about fighting than a gentleman who means to fight usually does. This article produced a challenge from the sub-lieutenant, who was named Courteil. When M. de Pene and his seconds got upon the ground they found some 10 officers there belonging to the garrison of St. Germain. The duel was fought with swords. M. de Pone wounded his antagonist in the wrist, and disabled him. Thereupon an officer of cuirassiers of the guard, named llyene, stepped out from the group, and said, " Now, sir, you will have to fight inc." The brave man of letters accepted this second challenge, although it was obvious that the men of the, sword had come out in great numbers with the deliberate intention of taking his life. In a few seconds he was run through the body Dr. Gucrin, who accompanied him from Paris, found it was impossible to stanch the blood. The wounded man was removed to a little inn at Pecq, near the railway, where, according to the latest intelligence, lie was lying with but a slight prospect of recovery. M de lb nc is not dead, and there is even some hope of his recovery, although he is said to be run through the lungs, liver and abdomen. By other accouuts it seems that a number of

S T . C ff 0, li X; A\ V l| S officers met at the Cafe du Holder, on the Boulevards des Italians, to discuss M. de Pene's articles in the Figaro, and there it was that a list was settled of the officers who were to call him out in succession. It is said that the names were written out on slips of paper, and that a colonel's hat was used to draw lots to see who should fight first 5!. do Tene's seconds were the Duke of Rovigo and M. l'eira, a Breton gentleman, who was formerly in the 3rd Guards of Charles X. lie was also accompanied to the ground by Doctor Guerin These four then found themselves in the face of 40. The officer with whom he first fought is a nephew of General Espinasse, the Minister of the Interior and Public Safety. When this officer received the wound which disabled his right arm, M. de Penc said a few words to him expressive of his sorrow for what had happened, assuring him that his article was not meant to be offensive. The combatants shook hands. The Duke of Ruvigo, thinking all was over, gathered up the swords, and was walking away with them off the ground, when another officer, stepping out from the group, struck M. do Pene on the face with his glove, and challenged him on the spot, llow it was that the seconds did not interfere to put a stop to this manifest butchery is not stated. Probably the second combat took place so rapidly and with such determination that they were unable to interfere. A Paris correspondent of the Nord, states that Madame de Pene arrived from Paris soon after the duel.

To some remarks from the seconds she replied, " For three days, gentlemen, T have been in agony." M Pene, it appears, had not concealed from her the fact that he was to fight a duel, and for three days the young lady had awaited with anxiety, the greater from the restrain in which it was kept, the end of this lugubrious drama. A correspondent states that at the very moment when the unfortunate man was lying without any apparent hope of recovery, two captains presented themselves, and demanded that M. de Penc should fight them They gave as their reason that they had been sub-lieutenant-.
