I stayed to hear no more, but drove the spur against the ribs of my horse, till he sprang iu j could reach its summit, the main body of the full gallop along the road. Eager as were my men to follow, 'twas as much as they could do to keep up. We no longer thought of scouts or cautious marching. The trappers had mounted, and were gallopiug with the rest. Wo thought only of time. We rode for the hacienda de Vargas, straight up the river. Although it was beyond the ranclieria, we could reach it without passing through the latter þÿ which lay some distance hack from the stream. We could return to the village afterwards, hut first for the hacienda. There I wished to arrive in the shortest time possible. The miles flow behind us, like the dust of the road. Oh, should wc not he in time ! I feared to calculate the length of the interval since the boy had hoard that rabble rout. Was it more than au hour r Five miles to the rancho, and he on foot. Hail lie travelled rapidly? . Yes, here and there ; hut he had made a stop : some men had passed him, and he had hidden in the hushes till they were out oi sight. He had been more than an hour ou the way nearly two, and one þÿ would be enough lor the execution of the darkest deed. Oh, we should not arrive in time ! There was no delay now. Wc were going at word. Alone might bo heard the clattering top-speed, ami in silence, scarcely exchanging of a hoofs, the chinking of bits, or the ringing of steel

scabbards. Neither the slimy gutter nor the deep rut of carreta wheels stayed our advance ; our horses leaped over, or went sweltering through them. In five minutes wo came to the rinconada , where the road forked þÿ the left branch leading to the village. We saw no one, and kept by on the right, the direut voad to the hacienda. Another mile, and wc should reach the house ; a its walls. On on ! sight of it ; the þÿ quarter of that distance, and wc should come of trees alone hindered our view in What means that light ? Is the sun rising in the west ? Is the chapparal on fire ? Whence comes the yellow gleam, half intercepted by the trunks of the trees ? It is not the moon ! ' Ho ! the hacienda is in flames !' ' þÿNo it cannot he ? A house of stone, with scarcely enough timber to make a blaze ! It cannot be that 3

It is not that. We emerge from the forest , the hacienda is before our eyes. Its white walls gleam under a yellow light of fire, but Dot of a conflagration. The house stands intact. A huge bonfire burns in front of the portal ; it was this that caused the glare through the forest. We draw up, and gaze upon it with surprise. We behold a huge pile þÿ the material supplied from the household stack of dry þÿfagots a vast blaze drowning the palo moonshine. Wo can rc:-; the hacienda, and all around it, as distinctly as by the light of day ! For what purpose this holocaust of crackling acacias 3 Around the fire we behold many forms, living and moving. There are men, women, dogs and saddled horses. Huge joints are roasting over the red coals, and others, roasted, are being greedily eaten. Are they savages who surround lhat blazing pile r No þÿ we can sec their laces with full distinctness, the white skins and black beards of the men, tlio cotton garments of the women ; we can see sombreros and scrapes, cloth cloaks and ealzoneros of velveteen, sashes and sabres; we can distinguish their voices as they shout, sing, and carouse ; we note their lascivious movements in the national dauce þÿ the jandango. No Indians they ! 'Tis a bivouac of the guerrilleros þÿ the ruffians for whom we are in search. 0 that I had listened to the voice of prudence, and adopted the strategy of a surround! Rut my blood was boiling, and 1 feared to lose even a moment of time, lest we might he too late. But one or two of my followers counselled delay,

and, as the event proved, they were the wisest. The rest, like myself, were impatient for action. The word was given ; and like houuds, fresh loosed from the leash, we rushed Co, ward with charging cheer. It was the madness of fools Well knew our enemy the hoarse Texan ' hurrah !' It had been shouted to terrify them, when there was no need. They would never have stood ground. The shout warned them, causing tin in to scatter like a herd of doer. The steep hill proved too heavy for our horses; and before we

guerrilla had inouutcd and scampered off into the darkness. Six of them tell to our shots, and as many more, with their she-associates, remained prisoners in our hands ; hut as usual lhat subtle coward had contrived to escape. Pursuit was idle ; they had taken to the dark woods beyond the hill. not 1 thought of pursuit ; my mind was bent on a different purpose. 1 rode into the patio. The court was lit up by the glare ol the tire. It presented a picture of ruin. Rich furniture was scattered about in the verandah aud over the pavement, broken or tumbled down. I called ber name þÿ the name ot Don Ramon. Loudly and earnestly did 1 raise iny voice, hut echo gave the only reply. I dismounted, and rushed into the verandah, still vociferating, and still without receiving a response. I hurried from room to room þÿ from cuarlo to sala þÿ from sala to sayuan þÿ up to the þÿazotea everywhere þÿ even to the capilla in the rear. The moonbeams gleamed upon the altar, hut no liutnau form was there. The whole house was deserted ; the domestics þÿ even the women of the cociua þÿ had disappeared. My horse and I seemed the ouly living things within those walls þÿ for my followers had remained outside with their prisoners. A sudden hope gleamed across my heart. Perhaps they had taken my counsel, aifd goue off before the mob appeared ? Heaven grant it might be so ! 1 rushed out to question the captives. Tbey should know, both men and women ; they could certainly tell me. A glance shewed mc I was too late to receive

information from the men. A large pecan tree stood at one corner of the buildiDg The firelight glared upon it ; from its branches hung six human forms with drooping heads, and feet fat from the earth. They had just ceased to live ! One told me that the herredero was among them, and also the cruel matador. Pedro had identified both. The others were peladns of the town, who had borne part in the affair of the day Their judges had made quick work, and equally quick had been the ceremony of execution. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 23rd JULY, 1858. We may be pardoned the presumption, in attempting to draw the attention of the authorities to a circumstance of vital importance to the interests of this community. Public opinion, in this, and the neighbouring Island, St. Thomas, seems, within the last few years, to have attained a degree of development, which, perhaps, is little suspected : and it often endeavours, despite the Censorship, to force an utterance in the columns of this paper and the St. Thomas Times. It is needless for us to disguise the fact, or for others to affect ignorance of it, that there exist public abuses, which ought to be exposed, in order to be removed. Unfortunately, although the Government, during the first Session of the Colonial Council, presented a draft to that Body, on the liberty of the Press, which contained these remarkable words in the preamble þÿ þÿ The latelyestablished representative Body, cannot dispense with that interchange of ideas, which can only be developed by a Free þÿPress þÿ yet the Home Government, refusing to abide by the advice of that Council, forbade the passing of the law ; and the press consequently still remains under Censorship. There is a rumour that an attempt has lately been made to establish a Press in the Island of Tortola, for the express purpose of furnishing a channel for the exposure of public abuses in these Colonies The authorities of that Island, grateful to our Government for the assistance rendered them during the rebellion in 1852, have signified their unwillingness to

grant the protection of their laws to a Press, the character of which, whether it may, or may not, be licentious or revolutionary in its tendency, they have no means to determine beforehand. The plan, we learn, has consequently been abandoned. We would now call the particular attention of the authorities to this circumstance : þÿ whether it were not the better course to furnish a channel for the expression of public opinion, under the protection and direction of our own laws, than to force it to seek such a channel in an alien Press ; where the pens of evil-disposed persons may find employment, free from the fear of any prosecution, except that, which would have to he carried on in a foreign conn try, and under difficulties and expenses tinthought of ? Governments have everything to gain and þÿ nothing Public and free þÿdeliberations, says an able to lose by the freedom of the Press authority, þÿ respecting the laws, measures and conduct of official persons art: sine to op rate in favour of the Government. If their position is not utterly untenable, it enables them to refute objections, to confound false reports, and to prove the necessity of the sacrifices required from the þÿpeople. A Press, governed by a law, similar to the one rccommcudcd by the Golonial Gouncil in 1852 would be of incalculable benefit to these Colonies; and we sincerely wish to see the subject meet that consideration which it demands.

Ripperger has solicited for leave of absence for 1 year; the memorial is recommended by the Schoolcommission, which has also recommended C. þÿWhispital s appointment as teacher at the school during the þÿpetitioner absence. s Replied, that the Council do not object to the arrangement, provided, however, that no additional expenses be incurred for the Land Treasury, if eventually it should be deemed requisite to make any other arrangement during Mr. þÿRipperger s absence. Proposal from the Policemaster at Chi i-

stiansted to have the well in New Street sunk s to 10 feet, assented to, provided that the work be done as economically as possible, and that ihe charges do not exceed the estimated cost $80. Memorial from Major Keutsch for leave of absence for 12 months, and that Examinatus juris J. Muller and Mr. F. Reports for assignment from : the Policemaster at the Centre District : selling licences issued in May $1. The Sheriff at Frederiksted : arrears of J school money for the 1st quarter $S 25. The Chairman produced copy of a representation to the Governor as agreed on in a special meeting of the Burgher Council on the 31st of May (at which meeting member Sarauw was absent on account of business) explaining the circumstances connected partly with the general mercantile crisis prevailing in Europe since last fall, partly with the small crop of this island in 1857, and the present ! indifferent prospects, which most seriously

affect the credit of a number of cane estates, and are likely to interfere with the payment j of the laborers and the supply of the corn meal absolutely required for their maintenance ; and recommending that the Burgher Council be authorized to advance

COMMUNICATIONS. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Dear Sir, The great diminution in the sale of Dry Goods, and other articles of usual consumption to the Labourers in the Country, has for some time past been seriously felt, and is universally complained of, by the shopkeepers in the Towns. This decrease notoriously arises from the numerous shops which, from time to time, have been opened in various parts of the Country, as well as from the almost universal practice of retailing Dry Goods in every hole and corner throughout the Country under the nose of the authorities, a fact which is undeniable, and palpable to every one but those whose duty it is to prevent this illegal traffic. The ordinance þÿ concerning Trades and þÿprofessions prohibits the sale of manufactured goods in the I Country, yet, what þÿManager house, s or other I principal Dwelling is there in the Country in which the retailing of dry goods, by some one or other connected with the establishment, is not more or less carried on ? The shops established about the Country on various Estates, ostensibly for the retail of Provisions &c., to the people residing on the property, form, as a natural consequence, a convenient cloak for carrying on such clandestine trade ; even the women who are permitted to þÿ þÿsquat ou Estates, under one cover or another, because they arc related to some of the Labourers employed on the property, þÿ almost universally retail some artieies of dry goods. The Ordinance þÿ with some trilling exception þÿ enacts

that þÿ Mercantile business shall only he carried ou in the þÿTown, and those who wish to qualify themselves for that purpose are obliged to incur the heavy expence of a Burgherbrief, or Licence, to which must he added various other expcuces incidental t>> their business, such as store rent, & , Ac. It must therefore he evident that it' the Labourers can obtain what they require in the Country the þÿshopkeeper s sale in Town must he commensurately reduced, and it is equally evident that they can not compete with those members named by the Council, and one | who can thus elude the Law and carry on trade without those charges on business to which the legal and authorised dealer is liable. One of the provisions of the ordinauce also enacts, that, þÿ the Polite shall officially attend to, re- i that no illicit traffic is carried on þÿ; hut how far they trouble themselves in this respect the foregoing facts may serve in some measure to illustrate. Vigilance and a penetrating eye, arc qualities usually supposed to be possessed by Police, but there are nono so blind as those who wont see, and it may he doubted from þÿwhat going s on whether their eyes are not often shut when they should ho open. I would also mention another practice equally unfair towards the shopkeepers in Town þÿ it is, that, persons frequently come over from 8t. Thomas with a variety of goods, hire a roomy Carriage into which they pack them, and drive about from one Estate to another, to dispose of them. The Town shopkeepers ought cither

or, by abrogating the Law, they should he placed on equal footing with those who carry on business in the Country, and if the sale of manufactured articles can not, or will not, be prevented, as complained of, it would only be fair to permit the þÿTowns people also to establish Shops in the Country, or send out itinerant sellers to vend their goods. Much more might he said upon this subject, but it is hoped that what is here stated at present may be sufficient to arouse attention in the proper quarter, and that we shall see such action taken in the matter as justice and respect for the laws demand, and, of those who the law as is rendered imperative by duty on the part says þÿ shall officially attend to. that no illicit traffic is carried þÿon. It appears that the que lion of the 1 .nulian Principalities may he considered as resolved, and a protocol containing the conclusions of the Conferences on the subje t is being drawn up, after which it will be discussed an signed, and the Plenipotentiaries will suspend their labours, probably until October, when they will meet again, to settle the questions still remaining undecided. I he intended visit of our gracious Queen to Cherbourg has called forth fervid compliments to her Majesty and to the English people from the French press The 1'atrie contains the following: þÿ "This new visit to I'N.uce of Queen Victoria will be regarded as a brilliant proof of the alliance which unites the two nations, and which has been considered by public opinion as menaced for a moment by recent events. It is. not to conclude a fresh alliance that the Queen of England will visit Cherbourg; her presence thcr will be a proof of the solidity of the alliance which exists, and which is necessary not only to the interests ot the two nations, but to the repose and prosp. rity of all Europe." MASSACRE OF CHRISTIANS AT JEDDAH. The following letter froui Alexandria, dated the 6th, gives some details of a massacre of Christians at Jeddah, the port of Mecca, on the Red Sea: þÿ About sunset on the loth of June the house of the English Vice-Consul at Jeddah was suddenly attacked, and invaded by some hundreds of liadramites (inhabitants ofSouthern Arabia), who seized the person of the Consul, wounded him grievously, and then fluug him, still alive, from the window into the street, where a niol> of the same fanatics hacked his body into pieces. The house was then pillaged ; the servants and two dragomen were assassinated, and the archives of the Consulate were burnt. \\ liilo this horrible scene was going on similar crimes were committed at the French Consulate. This Consul, also attacked by a hand of fanatics who penetrated into the house by the windows, fell mortally wounded by several sabre cuts. His wife was killed by a dagger thrust in her breast, alter having defended herself courageously, killed the murderer of her husband, and wounded several others. Her daughter, eighteen years old, succeeded in escaping by a secret door. In the next room were the Chancellor of the Consulate and his servant. This latter is a Mussulman, an old soldier who formerly >ci ved in a battalion of native Algerines. These two men and the Consul's young daughter defended themselves so heroically that the murderers retreated for a moment. They soon returned to the charge. One ot these wretches attacked the courageous

young girl, and gave her a sabre cut acro.-s the face. She fell senseless; but the Chancellor, whi! had sprung to his feet, inflicted a blow on the last assassin. Meanwhile the Chancellor's servant, struggling with admirable energy against these miscreants, killed three of them, wounded several others, and so succeeded in covering the flight of the Consul's daughter, ot the Chancellor, and of a servant, who linvo nil arrived this evening, in company with the brave, soldier, at the residence of the Consul- Ceneral of France in Alexandria While tlris carnage was going on all the Christians were as-ailed in the streets of Jeddah, and massacred. 1 wenty-three persons succeeded in escaping under cover of the night, and, throwing themselves into the sea, swain to the English steam dispatch-boat, which was at anchor in the port. All tiie other Christians, to the number of fortylive, have been killed and hacked in pieces. In the I. use of the brothers Suva, twelve persons (i: .iiillng the three brothers) have been murder i i. The number of Mussulmans who took part in the massacre is estimated at 5000. At the time of these occurrences the (Jovernor of Jeddah was at Mecca, with the troops under his command. He had left only 100 men in the garrison. At his return lie caused 300 of the assassins to be arrested, and he sent to the Christians who had taken refuge on board tin Cyclops a sum of 6000 piastres. The commander of this vessel has appointed Consuls ad interim, and proclaimed their installation

by a salute of guns. 1' he English flag was again hoisted, and the Turkish authorities attended the ceremony. Various reasons have been assigned for this fierce fanatical outbreak. The general opinion is that the event has been in preparation for a long time. The Arab population believes, in its ignorance, that since the Eastern war the influence of the Sultan is become greater than before. The populace sing ballads in Arabic and Turkish which breathe hatred of the Christians.

" That the exigencies of the country were and are such as to have induced your petitioners to look forward, as a last hope, to the arrival of a considerable number of agricultural labourers, whose presence and labour would mvc afforded the only relief from a state of things now tending to the early extinction of j Sugar and other cultivation throughout the island. That the disallowance of this Act has caused great dismay among your petitioners, inasmuch as it has destroyed their last remaining hope of being able to carry on cultivation, and thus must utterly rum their most vital interests. " Your petitioners, therefore, deem it their duty humbly to represent to your Excellency the above facts, and to pray that your Excellency may be pleased to consider the expediency of immediately convening the Legislature for averting, if possible, the present impending ruin, or for the adoption of such other measures as, in the judgment of your Excellency, may be i deemed necessary in the present emergency."

Wc knew whose throat he would have cut þÿ that of the Italianised Mexican taken at the mesa ; and I remembered that at the time of his capture su , had been Rube's advice, overruled, of course, by the more merciful of his comrades. 1 he trapper had assigned some reason : he knew something of the man's history. He uow repeated his reasons : ' He ur a true rennygade,' said ho ; an thur ain't on all the parairas a wusser enemy to whites than thctur þÿ more partiklurly to Texan whites.

He wur at the massacrce o' Wi son's family on the clur fork o' the Brazos, an wur conspik'us in tho skrimmigc : a' more too þÿ it ur thort he touted off one o' Wilson's guils, an made a squaw o' her, for he's mighty given that way I 've heern. Wagh ! he ur wuss than a Injuu, for the rcezun thet he unerstans the ways o' tho whites I never kuow'd sich a foolich thing as ter let 'itn git clur 'Eo may thank yur luck, Mister Stannafeel, thet he didn't take yur bar at the same time when he wur atakin o' yur hoss. ' Wagh ! thet ye may ! It was Stanfield's horse that had been stolen by the renegade, and the tracks now identified by the ranger were those of that animal þÿ no doubt with the freebooter upon his back. This new discovery let in a flood of light. Beyond a doubt, the war-t>arty was the same we hail met by tho mound, with perhaps a reinforcement ; the same thut had just plundered the Mexican town ; the samo who had paid their hurried visit to the hacienda, and this rene gadc Ha ! Strange remembrances were crowding into my brain 1 remembered meeting this semi-savage skulking about the road, after we had graDted him his parole ; I remembered.

upon one occasion, seeing him while riding out with her ; I remembered the rude expression with which he had regarded my companion þÿ the glance half-fierce, half-lustful ; I remembered that it made me angry ; that 1 rebuked and threatened him þÿ I now remembered all. Wild thoughts came rushing into my mind worse thoughts than ever. I sprang to my saddle, and, calling out some halfcoherent orders, rode rapidly along the trail. chapter i. xxvii. the writing on the maguey. The skill of the trackers was no longer called in need ; the war-trail was as easily followed as a toll-read : a blind man could havo guided himself along such a well-trodden highway. Our rate of speed was now ruled by the capacity of our horses. Alas ! their power was nearly at an end. They had been two days and a night under the saddle, with but a few hours to refresh themselves by food or rest : they could not hold out much longer. One by one they began to lag, until the greater number of them followed with tottering step hundreds of yards in the rear. It was in vain to contend against nature. The men were still willing, though they too were wearied to death ; but their horses were quite done up þÿ even whip and spur could force them no further. Only my own matchless steed could have continued the journey. Alono I might have advanced, but that would havo been madness. What could I have accomplished alone ? Night was fast coining down : it was already twilight. I saw by the clouded sky wc should have no moon. We might follow the trail with

our waxen torches not yet burnt out but that þÿ þÿ would no longer be safe. For myself, I was reckless enough to have risked life in any way, but the lives of my comrades were not mine. I could not give them þÿ I should not wastefully fling them away. Reluctantly 1 glided from my saddle, gave my steed to the grass, and sat down upon the earth. My followers coming up, said not a word but picketing their horses, seated themselves around me. One by oue they stretched themselves along the sward, and in ten minutes all were asleep. I alone could not sleep ; the fever of unrest was upon me ; the demon of thought would not let me close my eyes. Though my orbs ached with the long protracted vigil, I thought that ' not all the drowsy syrups of the world' could have given repose to my nerves at that moment. 1 felt as one who suffers under delirium, produced by the intoxicating cup, the fearful nianiaa-potu. I could neither sleep nor rest. I could not even remain seated. I rose to my feet and wandered around, without heed of where 1 was going. 1 strode over the recumbent forms of my sleeping companions; 1 went among the horses; f paced backwards and forwards along the banks of the stream. There was a stream þÿ a small arroyo or rivulet. It was this that had caused me to halt iu that particular spot ; for wild as were my thoughts, I had enough of rcasou left to know that wo could not encamp without water. The sight of the arroyo had decided my wavering resolution, and upon its banks, almost mechanically, I had

drawn bridle and dismounted. I once more descended to the bed of the stream, and, raising the water in the palms of my hands, repeatedly applied it to my lips and temples The cool liquid refreshed me, and seemed to soothe both my nerves and my spirit. After a time, both felt calmer, and I sat down upon the bank, and watched for a while the clear rivulet rippling past over its bed of yellow sand and glistening pebbles of quartz. The water was perfectly diapLanous ; and, though the sun silver-fish, of the genus hyodon sporting them- was no longer shining, could see tiny I . selves in the lowest depths of the pool. How I vnvied them their innocent gambols, their life of crystal purity and freedom ! Here, in this remote prairie-strcam, dwelt not the alligator, nor the ravenous garfish ; here came no dolphin or shark to chase them, no tyrant of the waters to put them in fear. To be envied, indeed, such an mcauciant, happy existence ! I watched thera for a long while, till 1 thought that my eyes were growing heavy, and, after all, T mijht sleep. The murmur of the arroyo

T\ & fk Q U k V I helped to increase this inclination to repose, and, perhaps, 1 might have slept; hut at that moment chancing to look around, my eyes fell upon an object that again drove sleep far away, and 1 was soon as wakeful as ever. Close to my elbow there I had seated myself þÿ grew large plant a of the Mexican aloe ( agave Americana ). It was the wild maguey, of course, but of a species with broad fleshy leaves of darkgreen colour, somewhat resembling the maguey of cultivation. I noticed that one of the great blades of the plant was bruised down, and the spine, which had terminated it, torn off'. All this would not have drawn my attention : 1 was already aware that the Indians had made a halt where we were encamped, and their sign was plenteous around þÿ iu the tracks of their animals, and the broken branches of trees. One of their horses or mules might have munched at the maguey iu passing, and, viewiug the bruised blade from a distance, 1 should have hazarded just such a conjecture. Rut my eyes were eloso to the plant, and, to nry astonishment, I observed that there was writing upon the leaf ! I turned over upon my knees, ana seizing the huge blade, bent it down before ure, so as to obtain a better view of its surface. I read : ' Captured by Comanches þÿ a war-party þÿ have many captives þÿ women and children þÿ ay de mi ! pobresninas! north-west from this place. Saved from death ; alas! I fear' The writing ended abruptly. There was no signature, but it needed not that. I had no doubts about who was the writer; in fact, rude as

was the chirography þÿ from the materials used þÿ I easily identified the hand. It was Isolina dc Vargas who had written. I saw that she had torn off the terminal spine, and using it as a stylus, had graven those characters upon the epidermis of the plant. Sweet subtle spirit ! under any guise I could have recognised its outpourings. 'Saved from death' þÿ thank Heaven for that! þÿ 'alas! I fear.' Oh, what feared 6hc ? Was it worse than death ? that terrible fate þÿ too terrible to think of? She had broken off without finishing the sentence. Why had sire done so ? The sheet was broad þÿ would have held many more þÿwords why had she not written more ? Did she dread to i the oauso of her fear ? or had she bceu interrupted bv i. approach of some ot her tyrant captors! O merciful Heaven! save me from thought! I re-read the words over and over : there was nothing more. I examined the other leaves of the plant þÿ on both sides, concave aud convex 1 examined them þÿ not a word more could I find : it was all she had written. chapter lxxviii. THE SOUTHERN SAVAGE. 1 need not tell how deeply 1 was affected by the unexpected communication. All at once were decided a variety of doubts ; all at once I was made aware of the exact situation. Isolina still lived þÿ that was no longer doubtful ; and the kuowlcdge produced joy. More than this : she was still uninjured þÿ able to think, to act, to write þÿ not only living, but well. The singular 'billet' was proof of all this. Another point þÿ her hat. is must have been fret þÿ her

hands at least, else how could she have traced those lines ? and with such a pencil 1 It argut . indulgence or tender treatment on the part of her captors Another point yet. She knew I was in pursuit She had seen me, then, as 1 galloped utter It was her cry I had heard as the steed dashed into the chappara). She had recognised me, and called back. She know I would still be following ; site kuew I was following, and for nte was the writing meant. Sweet subtle spirit ! Once more I devoured the welcome words ; but my heart grew heavy as I pondered over them. What had caused her to break off so abruptly 1 What was it her intention to have said ? Of what was she in fear ? It was my conjecture about this that caused the heaviness upon my heart. I gave way to horrid imaginations. Naturally my thoughts reverted to her captors ; naturally 1 reflected upon the character of the prairie savage þÿ so different from that of the forest Indian, opposite as is the aspect of their homes, and perhaps influenced by this very cause, though there are inary others. Climate

þÿ contact with Spanish civilisation, so distinct from Saxon þÿ the horse þÿ conquest over white foes þÿ concubinage with white and beautiful women, the daughters of the race of Andalusia : all these have combined to produce in the southern Indian a spiritual existence that more resembles Andalusia than England þÿ more like to Mexico than Doston or New York. There is not so much difference between Paris and the prairies, between the habitue of the R d Mabille and the horse-Indian of the plains. No cold ascetic this þÿ no romantic savage, alike celebrated for silence and continence þÿ but a true voluptuary, gay of thought and free of tongue, amorous, salacious, immoral. In nine cases out of ten, the young Comanche is a boastful Lothario as any flaneur that may be met upon the Roulevards ; the old, a lustful sinner þÿ women the idol of both. Women is the constant theme of their conversation, their motive of every act. 1" or them they throw the prairie dice; for them they race their swift mustangs. To win them, they paint a hideous guise ; to buy them, they steal horses ; to capture them, thev go to war ! And yet, with ail their v.' niton love, th y are true tyrants to the sex. Wife they have none þÿ noble lor it would be sheer sacrilege to apply this title to the ' squaw' of a Comanche, Mistress is scarcely a fitter tenn rather say slave. Here is a hard lot indeed : hers it is to hew the wood and draw the water ; to strike the teot and pitch it ; to load the horse and pack the dog; to

grain the skin and cure the meat ; to plant the maize, t ho melon, squash ; to hoc and reap them ; to wait obsequious on her lounging lord, anticipate his whim or wish, be true to him, or lose her cars or nose for sueh horrid forfeiture is, by Comanche custom, the punishment of conjugal infidelity ! But hard as is the lot of the native wife, harder still is that of the white captive 'Tis hers to endure all the ills enumerated, with still another þÿ the hostility of the squaw herself. Th i white captive is truly the slave of a slave, the victim of a treble antipathy þÿ of race, of colour, of jealousy. Oft times is she beaten, abused, mutilated ; and rarely d ies the apathetic loid i iterferc to protect her from this feminine hut ficndlike persecution. Tlicso were not imaginings ; they were not fancies begot in my own braiu. Would they had been so ! Too well did I know thev were facts þÿ horrid realities. Can you wonder that sleep was shaken from my eyelids ? þÿ that 1 could not think of rest or stay, til, I had delivered my loved one þÿ my betrothed þÿ from the danger of sueh a destiny : A!1 thought of sleep was banished þÿ even weariness forsook tne. I felt fresh as if 1 had slept; my nerves were strung for emprise. þÿ was excitement renewed by what I had read It the impatience of a new and keen apprehension I would have mounted and gone forward, spurning rest and sleep ; regardless of da -or would 1 have followed ; but what could I do alone ? Ay, and what with my few followers : H i! I

had not thought of this; up to that moment, T had not put this important question, and 1 had need to reflect upon the answer. What if we should overtake this baud of brizan Is ? Booty laden as they were, and cumbered with captives, surely we could come up with them, by night or by day ; but what then ? Ay, what tlieu ? There were nine of us, and we were in pursuit of a war-party of at least one hundred in number ! þÿ one hundred braves armed and equipped for battle þÿ the choice warriors of their tribe þÿ flushed with late success, and vengeful against ourselves on account of former defeat. If conquered, we need bok for no mercy at their hands ; if conquered þÿ how could it be otherwise' Nine against a hundred ! How could ice conquer ? Up to this moment, I had not thought of the result ; I was borne along by only one impulse þÿ the idea of overtaking the steed, and rescuing his rider from her perilous situation It was only within the hour that her peril had assumed a new phase ; only an hour since we had learned that she had escaped from one danger to be brought withiu tho influenoe of another. At first had I felt joy, but the feeling was of short existence. I recognised in tho new situation a greater peril than that she had outlived. She had been rescued from death to hecotno the victim of dishonour. T o be continued.

INDEMNITY FOR THE JEDDAH MAS- SACRE. Paris, Saturday. The Moniteur announces that the Governments of France and England have come to an understanding with the Porto with reference to the recent horrible events at Jeddah, with a view to due reparation. The conduct of the Ottoman authorities will be strictly inquired into ; and all guilty persons, of whatever rank, will he punished according to their deserts. Indemnities payable by the, towns which have had any share in the massacre will be given to all who have suffered cither in person or in property.

To prevent him from giving us further trouble, however, we tied him to a tree, iu such a manner that he could not possibly free himself. The mode of eccuriug him was suggested by þÿStanfie dthe backwoodsman : it was simple and sale. A tree was chosen, whose trunk was large et garnie avec les ! enough to fill the embrace of the savage, so that the ends of bis fingers just met when his arms were drawn to their full stretch around it. Upon his wrists, thongs of raw hide were firmly knot-

also bound by similar cords, the ends of which were staked, so as to hinder him from worming around the tree, and perchance wearing off his fastenings, or chafing them, so that they might break The ligature was perfect ; the most expert jail. breaker could not have freed himself from such a binding. It was our intention to leave him thus, and perhaps set him free upon our return, if wo should return by that þÿway a doubtful hypo thesis. I thought not at tho time of the cruelty we were committing. Wo had spared the þÿIndian s life a mercy at the moment and I was too þÿ þÿ much concerned about the future of others, to waste reflection on his. We had taken the precaution to leave him at some distance from the placo of his capture ; others of his party might come after, and discover him, soon enough to interfere with our plans. His prison had been chosen far off in the depth of the woods ; even his shouts could not have been heard by any one passing along the trail. He was not to be left entirely alone : a horse was to be his companion þÿ not his own þÿ for one of the rangers had fancied an exchange. Stanfield þÿ not well mounted þÿ proposed a 1 swop,' as he jocosely termed it, to which the savage had no alternative but consent; and the KcntuckiaD, having ' þÿhitched his worn-out nag to a tree, led off the skewbald mustang in triumph, declaring that he was now ' squar þÿwi tho þÿIndyens. Stanfield would have liked it better had the þÿswop been made with the renegade who had robbed him.

We were about to leave the place and move on, when a bright idea suddenly came into my head: it occurred to me that I too might effect a profitable exchange with our new-made captive a swop, not of horses, but of men þÿ in short, an exchange of persons þÿ of identities ! In truth, a bright idea it was, and one that promised well. I have said that I had already conceived a plan for the rescue ol my betrothed : I had done so during the night, and all along the route, in my mind I had been maturing it. The incident that had just transpired had given rise to a host of new ideas þÿ one, above all, that promised to aid me in facilitating the execution of my design. The capture of the savage, which had at first given me uneasiness, I now regarded in a very different light þÿ as a fortunate circumstance. I could not help thinking that I recognised in it the finger of Providence, and the thought ini spired mo with hope. 1 felt that I was not forsaken. The plan I had proposed to myself was simple enough ; it would require more of courage than stratagem ; but to the former I was sufficiently nerved by the desperate circumstances in which we had become involved 1 proposed to enter the Indian camp in the night þÿ of course, by I turned in my saddle, and glanced back ; I j stealth and under cover of the darkness þÿ to find the captive þÿ set her limbs þÿfree and then thrust

If once inside the encampment, and within reach of her, a sudden coup might accomplish all this : success was not beyond possibility, nor probability neither ; and the circumstances admitted of no plan that promised so fairly. To have fight with my few folsuch a host þÿ to have attacked the Indiau camp, even uuder the advantage of an alarm þÿ would have been sheer madness. It must have resulted not only in our immediate defeat, but would have destroyed our last chance of rescuing the captive. The savages once alarmed and warned, could never be approached again. Isolina would be lo.t lor ever. My followers agreed with me upon the imprudence of an attack. Folly they termed it; not from any motives of fear : they were willing to risk all ; and had 1 so ordered, would have charged with me, rifle in hand, into the very midst of the þÿenemy lines. every man of them. Even the voyageur the s 1 knew they would, þÿ least brave of my party þÿ would not have flinched; for, in the midst of brave meu, cowards cease to be. But such a course would indeed have been folly þÿ madness. Wo thought not of adopting it ; all approved of the plan I had formed, and which I had already sot before them as we tarried by the noon halting-place. Several had voluntcrccd to be my companions þÿ to venture along with me into the camp of the savages; to share with mo tho extreme of the danger; but for several reasons I was determined to go alone. Should even one of them be along with me, I saw it would double the risk of de-

tection. In this matter, stratagem, not strength, was needed, and speed in the last moments would be worth both. Of course, I did not expect to get tho captive clear without being observed and pursued þÿ that would have been prepo-terous ; she would be too well watched by tho savages þÿ not only by her jailers, but by the þÿjea ouseyes of those rival claimants of her body. No ; on the contrary, I anticipated pursuit þÿ close and eager ; it might be strife; but I trusted to my own swiftness of foot ; and to hers ; for well knew 1 her bold heart and free limb ; it was no helpless burden 1 should have to bring away. I trusted to my being able to baffle their pursuit þÿ to keep them back while she ran forward. For that purpose, I should take with me my knife and revolvers þÿ I trusted to these, and I much to chance, or, perhaps, I should rather say to God. My cause was good þÿ my heart firm and hopeful. Other precautions I intended to take : horses ready as near as they might be brought ; men also ready seated in their saddles, rifle in hand þÿ ready for fight, or flight. Such was the enterprise upon which I was resolved. Success or death was staked upon the issue. If not successful, I cared not to survive it. To be continued

The gratifying intelligence from India which we publish to day contrasts brightly with the dubious telegrams and desponding letters which have recently been received. It is true that the recapture of Gwalior by the forces under Sir Hugh Rose has been known to us for some days, but the details now given show how complete was the rout of the enemy, and lead that the moral effect victory must have been great and widely spread. It is needless for us to re capitulate the rebellious exploits of what was called the Gwalior Contingent It is sufficient to say that this force has shown a power of cohesion which has been wanting to almost every other hostile body. It received a severe blow from Sir Colin Campbell at Cawnpore, and suffered further from Sir Hugh Rose at the capture of Calpee; but it has yet been the nucleus of the army which, on the 2d of June, was strong

A great chief, perhaps the greatest in Central India, had been driven from his throne on account ot his fidelity to British rule. The successful rebels had, it is said, proclaimed Nana Sahib, assigned themselves six months' pay, and plundered a part of the city of Gwalior. To punish such outrages was a matter of immediate necessity. Happily this country has in its Indian Generals men whom numbers do not appal and difficulties do not discourage. Although the terrible sun of India side proachiug the solstice, and on every was ap- men and animals were sinking under the intolerable heat, the officers in command of the troops in Central India did not hesitate to press on and strike a decisive blow The battle in which Scindia was routed took place on the 2d, and on the 16th Sir II Rose reached Gwalior, at the same time that Brigadier Smith approached t from another quarter. 1 he enemy had eons ucntly but a short time to enjoy their triumph. The strength of the fort of Gwalior is been recently described in these columns, and our readers will consequently be better able to appreciate the skill and courage which were necessary for its recapture from a victorious and elated enemy.
